items.title: The movies of 2015
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
I absolutely love movie mashups.  Once nice aspect of a decade-old one is that by now I've seen a bunch of the relevant movies, and even a 2-second excerpt is enough to bring back pleasant memories.
I also use mashups to quickly scout for movies that might be of interest.  If you see a scene in the video and want to identify the movie, make a note of the time stamp and then look it up on this list.
I don't know how these are created; how does someone get access to so much material?  Then it requires a modicum of artistic vision to link the segments in various coherent ways.  I'll never have that skill or those resources, but perhaps TYWKIWDBI is in a way a "mashup" itself.

items.title: "Howcatchem" explained
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
I encountered "howcatchem" for the first time this past week, I think in a word puzzle somewhere.  Had to look it up, and found the answer in Wikipedia:
"An inverted detective story, occasionally known as a "reverse whodunnit" or "howcatchem", is a crime fiction structure in which the commission of the crime is shown or described at the beginning, usually including the identity of the perpetrator. The story then describes the detective's attempt to solve the mystery. There may also be subsidiary puzzles, such as why the crime was committed, which are explained or resolved during the story. This format is the opposite of the more typical "whodunit", in which all of the details of the perpetrator of the crime are not revealed until the story's climax. The first such story was R. Austin Freeman's The Case of Oskar Brodski published in Pearson's Magazine in 1912. The television series is one of the best-known examples of this genre."

Multiple famous examples are cited at the link.

items.title: Malian music
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
From reader soubriquet's blog Grit in the Gears comes this delightful videoThe musicians are Ali  Farka Toure -
Ali Ibrahim “Farka” Touré (October 31, 1939 – March 7, 2006) was a Malian singer and multi-instrumentalist, and one of the African continent’s most internationally renowned musicians. His music is widely regarded as representing a point of intersection of traditional Malian music and its North American cousin, the blues. The belief that the latter is historically derived from the former is reflected in Martin Scorsese’s often quoted characterization of Touré’s tradition as constituting "the DNA of the blues". Touré was ranked number 76 on Rolling Stone’s list of “The 100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time” and number 37 on Spin magazine's "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time".
-and Abdoulaye Diabaté.  I don't know what proportion of this piece is traditional Malian.  The language (Tuareg) certainly, the melody and rhythms probably.  But what fascinates me is how the incorporation of modern instrumentation and electronic modulation makes the music more "accessible" to my ear.

Not sure you'll like it?  Give it a click to start up while you scroll further down the blog.

items.title: 63 years ago today...
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
I remember exactly where I was.  I was on my high school's debate team and we were off at a tournament.  For practical reasons, our coach always drove us to tournaments; he would then serve as a judge on some of the debates not involving us, and we would all gather after the last debate of the day in some barren classroom to hear the results announced and get feedback on our performances. 

On that day, after the last afternoon debate, he didn't meet us.  After a brief search, we found him in his car, listening to the news on the car radio, in tears.  The news itself was startling, but the sight of encountering one of the pillars of the school faculty, our history teacher, unabashedly crying made the moment surreal for me.

As I was writing this, I decided to look up the National Forensic League's official debate topic for that year.  I remembered speaking as Second Affirmative, but didn't remember the topic.  Here it is:

1963-1964Resolved: That Social Security benefits should be extended to include complete medical care.
Wow.  How's that for a relevance stretching half a century into the future.  I wish I still had my file box of 3x5 cards.

Readers who have sharp memories of 11/22/63 are welcome to offer them in the Comments.

from 2013 to invite additional reflections and memories.

items.title: It never ends...
items.author: Minnesotastan
items.content:
After talking up this summit for months on end, it ended with no real accomplishments, and certainly not with the results Trump had hoped for. He had wanted to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons, but the three men left without announcing any agreement to end the fighting or reduce their nuclear arsenals. They did, however, manage to agree on something else. Trump, Xi, and Putin issued a joint declaration that called for protecting government officials from prosecution and limiting the power of the International Criminal Court, the court responsible for prosecuting some of the world’s worst crimes, including war crimes. Of all the things these three men could have agreed on, one of them was protecting government leaders from international prosecution. That is telling, although hardly surprising coming from them...
This morning, inside the Dirksen Senate Office Building, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is the agency responsible for helping protect American elections from cyberattacks and foreign interference, was asked a question that should have been incredibly easy to answer.  Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut wanted to know whether the United States Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. LoSapio said no, “I don’t believe it was an attack.” When Blumenthal pushed him further, LoSapio responded by claiming, “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” Then Blumenthal asked him who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election. Again, LoSapio refused to acknowledge what happened. “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. The man Donald Trump wants to put in charge of the federal agency responsible for helping protect our elections refused to acknowledge that the Capitol was attacked on January 6, and then refused to say who won the popular vote in 2020. Blumenthal looked at him and said, “You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill.”
He was not the only one today to deny or downplay what happened on January 6. Michael Chamberlain, who Donald Trump nominated to lead the Office of Government Ethics, the people who are supposed to hold public officials accountable, was asked the same question about January 6. He called it “behavior they shouldn’t have.” But he would not call it an attack or an insurrection, or even acknowledge what actually happened that day when a mob stormed the Capitol in an attempt to overturn an election...
During a separate hearing, just the day before, this time for a lifetime appointment to the federal judiciary, James P. Sullivan, a sitting justice on the Texas Supreme Court whom Donald Trump nominated to become a federal district judge in Texas, was asked whether Donald Trump could constitutionally run for president again in 2028. Sullivan initially struggled to even remember what the Twenty-second Amendment said, and Senator Chris Coons of Delaware had to help him. As Coons explained, the Twenty-second Amendment is very clear. It says a president who has been elected twice cannot be elected again. But when Coons asked Sullivan whether that meant Trump could not run again, Sullivan would not answer and called it an ongoing political debate. Senator Chris Coons told him, “That’s a very disappointing answer.”
